title: TypeScript SDK: Cross-runtime streaming shims and examples for Node/Deno/Browser
creator: Jordan Lee
acceptance_criteria: SDK exports light-weight helpers: toAsyncIterable(input), toWebStream(input), and consume(input, options)
Helpers accept Response, ReadableStream, AsyncIterable<string|Uint8Array|TokenChunk>, and Node Readable streams where possible
Cancellation via AbortSignal propagates from consumer -> SDK runtime -> underlying HTTP request (tested across Node/Deno/browser)
Backpressure guard: default in-memory buffer limited to configurable chunk count/bytes; documentation explains tuning and trade-offs
Integration examples for Node (undici/fetch), Deno, and browsers live in /examples/ts/streaming and CI exercise them
API surface documented with TypeScript typings and JSDoc, and migration notes for older Node versions
Automated tests cover: stream conversion correctness, cancellation propagation, simple memory bound scenario, and bundling smoke test
technical_design:
API surfaces: we will expose three small helpers: toAsyncIterable(input), toWebStream(input), and consume(input, {onToken, signal, maxBufferedBytes, maxBufferedChunks}).

- toAsyncIterable(input): returns AsyncIterable<TokenChunk> for input types: AsyncIterable, ReadableStream, Response, Node.Readable. Internally it normalizes bytes/strings to TokenChunk objects and yields them in canonical order. It wires an AbortSignal into the underlying reader, and exposes a close() method via a returned object when necessary (but primary surface is an AsyncIterable).

- toWebStream(input): converts the input to a browser-like ReadableStream<Uint8Array|string>. If the runtime already has native Web Streams, we use them; if not (older Node), we offer a tiny adaptor that delegates to node readable.pipeTo(new WritableStream(...)) behavior when polyfilled by the consumer. We will NOT inject a global polyfill.

- consume(input, options): high-level convenience that consumes any supported input and invokes onToken callbacks. It handles backpressure by awaiting the onToken promise and honoring maxBuffered* settings. It accepts an AbortSignal and ensures it cancels the underlying HTTP request.

Cancellation semantics: we propagate AbortSignal from caller to the request layer (fetch/undici/request). For Node.js undici pool, we call req.abort() and for fetch we pass the signal into the fetch init. If consumer aborts, we attempt graceful close (drain+close) and fall back to force abort. We record cancellation provenance in logs for debugging.

Backpressure/memory: default maxBufferedChunks=64, maxBufferedBytes=1_048_576 (1MB). These defaults balance latency and safety for typical chat workloads. We allow configuring via SDK client config or per-call options.

Types: use discriminated union TokenChunk = { type: 'text'|'delta'|'control', data: string|Uint8Array, meta?: string }. Keep types shallow to avoid deep nested generics. Provide helpful generics on consume<T> to allow typed structured outputs (for function calling scenarios).

Packaging: ESM entrypoint only (package.json: "module"). Provide small CJS bridge in separate file for legacy Node users, but recommend ESM. Rollup/tsup config will mark optional-deps like 'stream/web' as external to avoid bundling polyfills.
migration_notes:
- Node < 18: consumer must provide a Web Streams polyfill and/or pass a Node Readable to helpers. Document recommended polyfills (npm: web-streams-polyfill) and undici fetch shim.
- Deno: examples use global fetch and ReadableStream directly; no polyfills required.
- Existing SDK users who used raw Response/Readable in earlier SDKs should migrate by replacing direct iteration with toAsyncIterable(response) or consume(response, ...). Provide codemods in docs.
implementation_plan: Spike (1 day): prototype conversions for Response -> AsyncIterable and Node Readable -> AsyncIterable, measure overhead
API design doc + types (0.5d): finalize function signatures and defaults
Implement helpers (2d): toAsyncIterable, toWebStream, consume with cancellation/backpressure
Write integration examples (0.5d): Node/Deno/Browser examples in /examples/ts/streaming
Tests (1d): unit tests for conversions + cancellation + backpressure; add simple E2E using Playwright or node-fetch in CI
Docs & migration guide (0.5d): add to SDK docs and reference PR
Review + iterate (1d): feedback from SDK reviewers and infra; land PR and merge
test_plan: Unit: toAsyncIterable yields correct sequence for Response, ReadableStream, AsyncIterable, Node Readable
Unit: cancellation via AbortSignal results in underlying HTTP request aborted and iteration stops
Stress: bounded-buffer scenario where producer outruns consumer; verify memory stays under configured limits
Integration: example Node script consumes streaming chat and asserts ordering and token completeness
Cross-runtime: run browser example in Playwright, run Deno example in Deno test runner
Bundling: run tsup build and verify polyfill not pulled into main bundle (size regression test)
rollout_plan: Merge PR to main behind feature flag `ts_stream_shims`
Publish beta SDK release (tag: beta-ts-stream-shims) and ask internal partners to try examples
Monitor usage via early adopters, collect feedback for 2 weeks
Flip feature flag and include helpers in stable release sdk-ts-2025.03 if no major issues
risks: Runtime fragmentation: too many runtime-specific edge cases increase maintenance burden
Bundle size: accidentally pulling polyfills into main SDK could bloat bundle for browser consumers
Cancellation mismatch: some HTTP client libraries don't expose abort semantics cleanly; implementing consistent behavior will require adapter code
Testing matrix: ensuring reliability across Node versions, Deno versions, and browsers is time-consuming
decisions: Do not auto-polyfill Web Streams. Provide clear docs and opt-in polyfill guidance. (Trade-off: smaller SDK vs more developer setup for old runtimes)
Expose small set of helpers instead of a single monolithic conversion API to keep ergonomics explicit and typed
Default buffered limits: 64 chunks / 1MB; configurable by users
ESM-first packaging with a tiny CJS bridge for legacy users
open_questions: Should we expose a combined TransformStream utility that applies token delimiting and simple token merging (helps some customers but increases API surface)?
Do we want to include helper adapters for common fetch shims (undici) to simplify Node bootstrap?
Is the default buffered byte limit appropriate for long-token outputs like embeddings or should we reduce it?
progress_updates: 2025-01-09: Created spike PR and verified Response -> AsyncIterable conversion works for small test server (prototype code in /tmp)
2025-01-14: Implemented initial toAsyncIterable + consume helpers; added basic unit tests for the Node/Response paths
2025-01-22: Design review with SDK owners. Feedback: add explicit onBackpressure callback and ensure typed TokenChunk shape. Updated types accordingly.
2025-02-03: Added Deno and browser examples. Found subtle behavior difference in ReadableStream.defaultReader().read() when returning done:true; adjusted adapter to close iterator correctly.

2025-02-10: Internal PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-js/pull/9876 (WIP). Requesting SDK eng review. CI failing on Playwright test flakiness; investigating network timing in Playwright VM.
2025-02-19: Addressed review comments (narrowed exported surface, added docs, improved cancellation logging). Preparing for beta publish.
notes_for_reviewers: Please focus on: cancellation correctness across runtimes, clarity of types for token vs structured responses, and any packaging concerns that might pull polyfills into the main bundle. For reviewers on Windows CI: the Playwright network timing tests are flaky; prefer local runs to validate logic before approving.
final_notes: This approach keeps the SDK small while addressing the majority of developer pain points around runtime differences. If adoption shows many users rely on older Node without polyfills, we can re-evaluate providing an opt-in compat bundle in a separate package.
